title: Errors in a CRM
metaTitle: Errors in a CRM, said plainly
excerpt: When a save fails between calls, say what broke and what to do next. An error code and a sad illustration waste the only moment that matters.
alt: A white geometric building with a glass wing and a cantilevered upper volume, a structure whose load has to be obvious to read.
caption: A geometric building with a glass wing, structure you can actually see. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a CRM error say?
faqs.answer: Say what broke, whether the note was kept, and what to do next, in the salesperson's words. Name the field or the conflict if you know it. An error code, a sad illustration, and a generic 'something went wrong' waste the moment between calls.

faqs.question: Should we show error codes at all?
faqs.answer: You can keep a code for support, small and secondary. The sentence the salesperson reads should not depend on it. If they need a code to be helped, the copy has failed. Support can ask for the code after the person knows their note is safe.

faqs.question: What if the failure is actually a permission?
faqs.answer: Say that. 'You can draft this note, but only the account owner can change the stage' is an error that tells the truth. Hiding the control, or failing with a generic message, feels like a bug. Send them to the next action they are allowed to take.

markdown:
CRM error states have one job between calls: say what broke and what to do. The salesperson updating a record does not have time to interpret a code, and they should not have to admire a sad illustration while the next call starts. The note is either safe or it is not. The screen has to say which.

A vague failure is how a CRM trains people to keep the truth in a notebook instead.

## The moment the save fails

They pressed the verb you offered them. Log the call. Save the note. The product asked for that tap and then refused it. This is the most fragile second in the session, because the person did the right thing and the system dropped it. Your tone should be plain and specific. No joke. No character. No "oops."

Start with the fate of the words they typed. "Your note is still on this page. It was not saved to Northwind." That sentence is worth more than any diagnostic. If you can say it, say it first. If you cannot say it because you are not sure, find out. Shipping an error that might have saved and might have lost the note is worse than a slower save that tells the truth.

Then say what broke, as far as you know, and the next action. "The stage could not change because the deal is closed. The note can still be saved." Two sentences. A button that does the possible thing. The impossible thing should look unavailable, with the reason beside it, not like a second error waiting to happen.

[The WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes a standard organized under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. An error is an understandable-and-operable moment. The person has to perceive what happened, understand it in text, and operate a way forward. A toast that vanishes, a red border with no words, or a code that only engineering knows are failures of that standard even before you score a formal audit. WCAG applies to web applications, not only to marketing pages. A CRM is a web application. Write the error as if a keyboard user and a screen-reader user will meet it on a phone in a hallway, because they will.

## Say what broke in their words

Translate the failure. A required field is "Add the company name to save." A conflict is "Sam updated this deal while you were writing. Here is their note. Yours is kept below." A network failure is "You are offline. The note is on this device and will save when you reconnect." A validation rule is "The close date is in the past. Pick a new date, or save the note without changing the date."

None of those sentences required the reader to know what a 422 is. If you must show a code for the support desk, put it in small type after the sentence, or behind "details." The sentence is the interface. The code is a serial number.

Do not blame the user. "Invalid input" blames them for a rule they could not see. Name the rule. Do not blame "the system" in a way that gives them nothing to do. "The system is unhappy" is a mood, not an instruction. Say the next tap.

Field-level errors belong on the field. A banner at the top of a long record that says "fix the highlighted errors" is a scavenger hunt. Highlight, and write the sentence at the field. If several fields failed, list them in the banner as links that move focus. A salesperson between calls will not scroll a record looking for a red asterisk they might have missed.

## What was kept

Preservation is the feature. Autosave drafts locally when the network is the problem. Keep the text in the field when the server rejects a field. Never clear the form on failure. Clearing the form is a second, worse bug wearing the first bug's coat. People will tell you, once, and then they will paste notes into a chat with themselves.

If you did save part of the change, say which part. "The note was saved. The stage was not, because the deal is closed." Partial success that looks like total failure makes people retry and duplicate the note. Partial success that looks like total success makes the stage wrong and the forecast wrong. Distinguish them in the first line, not in a paragraph below a fold.

Conflicts need both versions visible. Theirs and Sam's. A modal that says "overwrite or discard" without showing Sam's text is how the quieter update gets destroyed. Between calls, the salesperson will choose overwrite every time, because discard sounds like losing their own words. Show the words. Then offer "keep both" as the default. Overwrite can exist. It should not be the path of least reading.

## Why a code and an illustration fail

A code fails because it names the product's internal category, not the user's situation. "Error CRM-1042" cannot tell them whether to wait, to edit a field, or to call Sam. It sends them to a help center they will not open. It also looks unfinished, which is ironic, because teams add codes to look serious. Serious is a sentence.

A sad illustration fails because it spends the moment on a feeling. A crumpled paper, a disconnected plug, a small character frowning. The feeling is already obvious. The salesperson is annoyed. The illustration confirms the annoyance and delays the instruction. It also tends to replace the text, which fails anyone who does not see the picture the way you intended. Put the sentence first. If you have room for a drawing, you have room for the next step, and the next step should take the room.

Humor fails here for the same reason. A witty 404 on a marketing site can be a small pleasure. A witty save-failure in a CRM is a colleague laughing while your note hangs. Match the stakes. The stakes are a lost fact about a buyer.

Retry without an explanation fails too. A button that says "Try again" and does the same request, against the same rejection, is a loop. Only offer retry when something might have changed: the network, a lock, a moment later. If the input is wrong, the button should be "Save without the close date" or "Edit the date," not a blind retry.

## The errors that actually happen between calls

Design these before you design the rare ones.

Offline, because they are in a building with bad reception and the note is the whole point. Required fields that were not required a second ago, because a stage change revealed them. Permission to edit the account but not the amount. A duplicate person, because the buyer spelled their email two ways over the years. A record someone else deleted. A file too large, if you let them attach the deck. A session that expired while they were on the phone, which must not throw away the note to send them to a login screen with nothing in its pockets.

For each one, write the three lines: what broke, what was kept, what to do. Put them in the component, not in a wiki. If a new failure mode ships without those three lines, it is not ready. Engineering can still log the technical cause. The interface has a different audience.

Session expiry deserves a special rule. Authenticate again in a layer, then return them to the same record with the draft. A full-page login is how drafts go to die. If your stack cannot do that yet, do not pretend the error copy can compensate. Fix the return path. Copy is not a substitute for getting them back to the object.

## Errors that are really permissions or search

Some failures are not failures of the save. They are failures of expectation. The rep cannot edit the field because it belongs to finance. The rep cannot find the account because it lives under a different name. Do not use the generic error component for these. A permission needs the reason and the person who can help, without making the rep file a ticket to learn a policy. A missing record needs the search you should have offered, with the query they already typed.

If everything becomes an "error," the word stops meaning anything and people click through it. Reserve the error treatment for "this action did not happen." Use a quieter explanation for "this action is not yours." The next pieces in the work are those two cases. Here, keep the boundary sharp so the save failure stays unmistakable.

Test the copy by reading it to someone who did not build it, with the code hidden. Ask them what they would tap. If they hesitate, the sentence is still about you. Rewrite until the tap is obvious. Then test it with a screen reader and with the page zoomed. The error text has to be in the DOM, next to the field, not only in a color or a toast that disappears while they are still on the call.

## A short review before you ship

Read every error the CRM can throw on this flow. Reject any that are only a code, only a color, or only an illustration. Reject any that clear the form. Reject any joke. Time the recovery the way you timed the first screen: the note should be safe, and the next legal action visible, inside the same short gap.

This is craft, not a phase you add after the happy path. The happy path is a demo. The error path is the product on a Thursday.

When the failure is "you are not allowed," the copy changes again. [Permissions in a CRM](/blog/permissions-in-a-crm) is the next piece, because a hidden button feels like a bug, and the salesperson needs to see what they can do and why the rest is unavailable.

If you want these states designed with the same care as the happy path, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring one failed save your team currently explains with a code.
